title: Kierkegaard: Faith, Anxiety and the Individual
subtitle: No system can live your life for you
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why Kierkegaard rebelled against Hegel's 'System' and championed the single individual
Describe the three stages or spheres of existence: aesthetic, ethical and religious
Explain Fear and Trembling's reading of Abraham, including the 'teleological suspension of the ethical' and the knight of faith
Explain what Kierkegaard meant by anxiety, despair and the claim that 'subjectivity is truth'
Weigh the strongest objections to Kierkegaard and see why he is called the father of existentialism
hook:
Copenhagen, autumn 1841. A thin, sharp-tongued young theologian named Søren Kierkegaard has just broken off his engagement to Regine Olsen, an eighteen-year-old he adored. He had proposed a year earlier and she had said yes. Now, for reasons he never fully explained, he hands back the ring, plays the cad in public so that she will think him a scoundrel rather than pity him, and sails for Berlin. There he sits in the lecture hall of the famous philosopher Schelling, alongside, as it happens, a young Friedrich Engels and the anarchist Mikhail Bakunin. He comes home disappointed and starts writing at a furious pace.

For the rest of his short life Kierkegaard circled one question: how should *I* live? Not "what is the good life for human beings in general?" but what am *I*, this particular person with this particular history, supposed to do with my one existence? Remember Hegel on Day 59, who saw history as the grand self-unfolding of Spirit? Kierkegaard thought that a philosophy which can explain the whole of world history but cannot tell you whether to marry Regine has forgotten the most important thing of all.

sections.heading: A Strange Life in Golden-Age Copenhagen
sections.body:
Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813, the youngest of seven children of Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard, a wealthy wool merchant who had grown up as a poor shepherd boy on the heaths of Jutland. The father was devout, brilliant and gloomy. Søren later recorded in his journals a family story that the father, as a hungry boy, had once stood on a hill and cursed God, and carried the guilt of it for life. Five of the seven children and the mother died before Søren was twenty-two, and the father seems to have believed the family lay under a curse. Søren inherited both the money and the melancholy.

He studied theology at the University of Copenhagen, slowly, while living as a well-dressed man about town. In 1841 he completed his dissertation, *On the Concept of Irony with Continual Reference to Socrates*. That subtitle matters: Socrates (Day 9) was Kierkegaard's lifelong hero, the thinker who refused to hand people ready-made answers and instead forced them to examine themselves.

After the broken engagement came an astonishing burst of writing. Between 1843 and 1846 he published *Either/Or*, *Fear and Trembling*, *Repetition*, *Philosophical Fragments*, *The Concept of Anxiety*, *Stages on Life's Way* and the huge *Concluding Unscientific Postscript*. Most appeared under playful pseudonyms such as Johannes de silentio ("John of silence") and Johannes Climacus ("John the Climber"). In 1846 he picked a fight with *The Corsair*, a satirical paper, which responded by caricaturing his thin legs and uneven trousers until street boys mocked him by name.

In his final years he turned his fire on the Danish state church, arguing in a pamphlet series called *The Moment* that comfortable, official "Christendom" had quietly abolished real Christianity. In October 1855, in the middle of this campaign, he collapsed in the street. He died in November, aged forty-two, refusing communion from a priest of the church he had attacked. He was largely unknown outside Denmark until German translations made him famous in the early twentieth century.

sections.heading: Against the System: The Single Individual
sections.body:
In the 1830s and 1840s Hegel's philosophy dominated Copenhagen's intellectual life. Hegelians spoke of "the System," an all-embracing account in which every idea, every era and every individual found its place as a moment in the development of Absolute Spirit. Kierkegaard found this both comic and dangerous.

It was comic because the system-builder forgets that he himself exists. Kierkegaard compared such a thinker to a man who builds an enormous palace but lives in the shed next door. The theory is magnificent; the theorist's actual life is untouched by it. It was dangerous because it encouraged people to see themselves as mere examples of a general type: a citizen, a member of the age, a Christian simply because they were born in Denmark. The System could tell you where you fit in world history. It could not tell you what to do on Tuesday.

Against this Kierkegaard set **the single individual** (*den Enkelte*), the concrete, existing person who must make choices that no theory can make for them. "Existence" for Kierkegaard is not a bare fact, like a rock existing. To exist as a human being is to be unfinished, to be always in the process of becoming, and to be responsible for what you become. One of his best-known journal entries (from 1843) captures the predicament: life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.

He was equally suspicious of the crowd. In a note written in the late 1840s he declared that "the crowd is untruth": not because ordinary people are stupid, but because in a crowd nobody is responsible. Opinion, the press and public mood let each person hide behind "everyone." (Heidegger will develop this idea as "das Man," the anonymous They, on Day 76.)

This is also why he wrote under pseudonyms. He called his method **indirect communication**. If you simply tell someone the truth about how to live, they will nod, file it away and change nothing. So instead he created characters who embodied different ways of living and let readers confront them, as Socrates did, and work out the answer for themselves.

sections.heading: Either/Or: The Aesthetic and the Ethical
sections.body:
*Either/Or* (1843) is presented as a bundle of papers found in a second-hand desk by an editor called Victor Eremita. The first half is written by a young man known only as "A"; the second half by an older civil servant, Judge William. Together they introduce what Kierkegaard later called the stages or spheres of existence.

The **aesthetic stage** is a life lived for interest, pleasure and the avoidance of boredom. "Aesthetic" here does not just mean loving art; it means living by what is immediately appealing. The aesthete may be crude, chasing pleasures, or extremely refined, a witty connoisseur of moods. A's essays are dazzling. In one, "The Rotation of Crops," he argues that boredom is the root of all evil and offers techniques for keeping life interesting: never commit, never make friends you cannot drop, treat life as a series of experiences to be savored. The book ends A's papers with "The Seducer's Diary," a chilling account of a man who engineers a young woman's love purely for his own enjoyment and then abandons her.

What's wrong with this life? Not that it is unpleasant, but that it has no center. The aesthete is scattered across his moods, always waiting for the next interesting thing. Underneath the wit, Kierkegaard suggests, lies **despair**: a self that has never actually become a self.

Judge William answers in long, warm, slightly pompous letters. He urges A to enter the **ethical stage**: to choose himself, to take responsibility for his life, to commit to duties, work and, above all, marriage. The ethical person gives life continuity. A promise made today binds me tomorrow; I become someone with a history I own. The judge's key point is that the real choice is not between good and evil but between choosing and not choosing. The aesthete has not chosen evil; he has avoided choosing at all.

Notice that Kierkegaard does not tell us who wins. The book's title is a demand: *either* this *or* that, and you, reader, must decide. Later works add a third sphere, the **religious stage**, which neither A nor the judge fully understands, and which brings us to Abraham.

sections.heading: Fear and Trembling: Abraham and the Leap
sections.body:
In Genesis 22, God commands Abraham to take his son Isaac, the son he waited for all his life, up Mount Moriah and sacrifice him. Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey, makes the three-day journey, binds Isaac and raises the knife. Only then does an angel stop him, and a ram is sacrificed instead. Preachers in Copenhagen told this story every year as a comforting tale of faith rewarded. Kierkegaard's pseudonym Johannes de silentio, in *Fear and Trembling* (1843), insists that if we actually think about it we should be horrified. Ethically described, Abraham was willing to murder his son.

So either Abraham is a murderer, or there is something higher than ethics. Johannes calls this possibility the **teleological suspension of the ethical**: a suspension of universal moral rules for the sake of a higher end (*telos*), namely a person's absolute relation to God. Ethics, in Hegel's and Kant's sense, is universal: it is what anyone in my position ought to do, and it can be explained and justified to others. Abraham cannot explain himself. He is silent on the journey; he cannot even tell Sarah or Isaac. That is why his situation is one of fear and trembling.

Johannes contrasts two figures. The **knight of infinite resignation** gives up what he loves most, accepts its loss, and finds a kind of painful peace. Johannes says he can understand this and even imagine doing it. The **knight of faith** does something stranger: he gives up everything and, at the same moment, believes that he will receive it back, in this life, "by virtue of the absurd." Abraham surrenders Isaac and yet believes he will keep Isaac. Johannes admits he cannot make this movement himself. Wonderfully, he adds that a real knight of faith might look entirely ordinary, like a tax collector enjoying his Sunday dinner.

This is where the famous phrase **leap of faith** comes from, though, as scholars like to point out, Kierkegaard never actually uses that exact expression. He speaks of the "leap" (*Springet*) and of faith as a decision that no amount of evidence or argument can force. You cannot reason your way step by step into faith, as Aquinas's Five Ways (Day 35) might suggest. At some point you must leap, with no guarantee.

sections.heading: Anxiety, Despair and the Dizziness of Freedom
sections.body:
Kierkegaard was one of the first great psychologists of the inner life, and two of his books gave lasting names to experiences everyone has.

In *The Concept of Anxiety* (1844) he distinguished **anxiety** (*Angest*, often translated "dread") from fear. Fear has an object: a snarling dog, a failing grade. Anxiety is directed at nothing in particular; it is a response to *possibility* itself. Kierkegaard's image is a person standing at the edge of a cliff. He is afraid of falling, but he also feels the strange pull of the thought that he *could* jump. Nothing stops him except himself. In a much-quoted line, Kierkegaard calls anxiety "the dizziness of freedom."

This is a striking reversal. Anxiety is not just a malfunction to be removed; it is the sign that you are a free being, facing a future that is genuinely open. An animal does not feel it, and neither, Kierkegaard says, would an angel. He even suggests that learning to be anxious in the right way is an education: whoever has learned it rightly "has learned the ultimate."

In *The Sickness unto Death* (1849) the subject is **despair**, and the analysis goes deeper. A human self, he says, is not a thing but a relation: a tension between the finite and the infinite, necessity and possibility, what you are given and what you might become. Despair is a disorder in that relation. It comes in forms such as not wanting to be a self at all, losing yourself in the crowd and its routines, or desperately wanting to be a self of your own invention, cut off from anything greater. Most troubling of all, Kierkegaard claims that the most common form of despair is not knowing that you are in despair. The busy, successful person who has never asked who they are may be the most lost of all.

For Kierkegaard the cure is not therapy but faith: a self that rests, transparently, in the power that established it, which for him meant God. But even readers who reject his Christianity have found his map of anxiety and self-deception uncannily accurate.

sections.heading: Subjectivity Is Truth, and the Objections
sections.body:
In the *Concluding Unscientific Postscript* (1846), Johannes Climacus makes his most notorious claim: **subjectivity is truth**. This sounds like crude relativism, "whatever I feel is true for me," but that is not what he means.

Climacus distinguishes two kinds of question. Objective questions, in mathematics, history or science, are answered by looking away from yourself at the evidence; your passion is irrelevant to whether a theorem is valid. But some truths concern how you exist, and for those, *how* you hold a belief matters as much as *what* you believe. He gives a deliberately shocking example: imagine someone in Christendom who prays to the true God but in a false, merely conventional spirit, and an idolater who prays to an idol with the whole passion of the infinite. Which one, he asks, has more truth? His answer is the idolater. Truth in the existential sense is a matter of passionate, inward commitment, not of reciting correct propositions. Here again we hear the young man at Gilleleje who wrote in his journal in 1835 that he needed to find a truth which is true for him, the idea for which he could live and die.

The objections are serious:

- **Fanaticism.** If faith may suspend ethics, how do we tell Abraham from a man who kills his child because voices told him to? Kierkegaard's defenders say his whole point is that you *cannot* tell from outside, which is why he calls it terrifying, not admirable. Critics reply that a philosophy with no public check on such claims is dangerous.
- **Irrationalism.** Does the leap abandon reason? Some readers think Kierkegaard used reason with great rigor to show where reason runs out; others see a retreat from argument. Camus (Day 79) will call the leap a form of "philosophical suicide."
- **Individualism.** By isolating the single individual before God, does Kierkegaard neglect community, politics and our responsibilities to one another? Marx (Day 63), writing at the same time, would have found the whole project hopelessly private.

Still, his influence is enormous. Heidegger (Day 76), Sartre (Day 77) and Camus all built on his themes of anxiety, choice and authenticity, which is why Kierkegaard is often called the father of existentialism, a label he never used. Tomorrow we meet the other great nineteenth-century rebel against comfortable Christianity, who reached the opposite conclusion: Nietzsche.

keyQuote.text: It is perfectly true, as philosophers say, that life must be understood backwards. But they forget the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.
keyQuote.source: Søren Kierkegaard, Journals (1843), trans. Alexander Dru

modernConnection.title: The Dizziness of Infinite Options
modernConnection.body:
Kierkegaard would recognize our world instantly. Think of the endless scroll: a fresh supply of the interesting, the funny and the outrageous, perfectly designed to keep boredom at bay. His aesthete "A" spent his days rotating moods and amusements; we have apps that do the rotating for us. Many people describe a peculiar emptiness after hours of this, a sense of having been entertained without having lived. That is very close to what Kierkegaard meant by aesthetic despair: not misery, but a life without a center, spread across experiences that never add up to a self.

His analysis of anxiety also speaks to modern life. Psychologists such as Barry Schwartz have written about the "paradox of choice": more options can make people less satisfied and more paralyzed, because every choice closes off others. Young adults facing unlimited possible careers, partners, cities and identities often report exactly Kierkegaard's dizziness. The freedom is real, and that is precisely what makes it frightening. Some existential psychotherapists, influenced by Rollo May and others, draw directly on Kierkegaard to treat anxiety not only as a symptom to suppress but as a signal about what matters to you.

And Judge William's message, that the real choice is between choosing and not choosing, is a pointed challenge to a culture of keeping options open: the dating app swipe that never settles, the half-commitment, the "let's see what else comes along."

But the comparison has limits. Clinical anxiety disorders are medical conditions with biological components and effective treatments; it would be cruel to tell someone with panic attacks that they simply need to leap. Kierkegaard's own answer to despair was specifically Christian faith, which many modern readers do not share. And he was writing for a small, educated, prosperous audience; for people struggling to meet basic needs, the problem is often too few options rather than too many. What survives is his insight that freedom is not only a gift but a weight, and that no app, crowd or system can carry it for you.

vocabulary.definition: Kierkegaard's term (den Enkelte) for the concrete, existing person who must make his or her own choices, as opposed to an abstract member of a group or a moment in a system.
vocabulary.example: Kierkegaard dedicated several works to 'that single individual,' the one reader who would take the book personally.

vocabulary.definition: A way of life organized around pleasure, interest and avoiding boredom, without lasting commitment.
vocabulary.example: Someone who changes jobs, partners and hobbies the moment they become dull is living in the aesthetic stage.

vocabulary.definition: A way of life in which a person chooses himself or herself and takes on lasting duties, commitments and responsibility.
vocabulary.example: Judge William's praise of marriage as a daily, freely renewed promise is Kierkegaard's portrait of the ethical stage.

vocabulary.definition: The highest sphere of existence for Kierkegaard: a passionate, personal relation to God that cannot be reduced to universal ethical rules.
vocabulary.example: Abraham on Mount Moriah is Kierkegaard's most extreme image of the religious stage.

vocabulary.definition: A commitment that cannot be reached by evidence or argument alone but requires a decisive choice; Kierkegaard spoke of the 'leap', though not this exact phrase.
vocabulary.example: No proof could make her believe, so she described her conversion as a leap of faith.

vocabulary.definition: The idea in Fear and Trembling that universal moral rules might be set aside for a higher end, namely an individual's absolute duty to God.
vocabulary.example: Johannes de silentio asks whether Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac is murder or a teleological suspension of the ethical.

vocabulary.definition: A dread directed not at a specific object but at possibility and freedom itself; 'the dizziness of freedom.'
vocabulary.example: Standing before a blank future with every door open, he felt not fear of something but anxiety about everything he might become.

vocabulary.definition: Kierkegaard's method of writing through pseudonymous characters and stories so that readers must work out the truth for themselves rather than passively receive it.
vocabulary.example: Because of indirect communication, you cannot assume that anything Judge William says is simply Kierkegaard's own view.

thinkingExercise.title: Which Stage Are You In?
thinkingExercise.prompt: Kierkegaard believed you cannot understand his stages from the outside; you have to locate yourself in them. Take 10 to 15 minutes to examine one area of your own life using his map.
steps: Pick one important area of your life: work, a relationship, your use of free time, or your beliefs.

Describe honestly how you approach it. Where do you act for interest and pleasure (aesthetic)? Where do you act from commitment and duty you have chosen (ethical)? Is there anything you hold with a passion that goes beyond what you could justify to others (religious, in a broad sense)?
Judge William says the real choice is between choosing and not choosing. Write down one thing you are avoiding deciding, and what keeping that option open is costing you.
Recall a moment of anxiety in Kierkegaard's sense, dizziness before an open possibility rather than fear of a specific danger. What did it reveal about what you care about?
Finally, play the critic: write two sentences on where Kierkegaard's framework does not fit your experience or seems mistaken.

summary: Kierkegaard (1813–1855) rebelled against Hegel's all-embracing System, insisting that philosophy must address the single, existing individual who has to choose how to live.
He wrote through pseudonyms (indirect communication) to force readers to decide for themselves, much as Socrates did.
His three stages of existence are the aesthetic (pleasure and interest), the ethical (chosen commitment and duty) and the religious (an absolute personal relation to God).
Fear and Trembling uses Abraham to ask whether faith can involve a 'teleological suspension of the ethical'; the knight of faith gives everything up yet believes he will receive it back.
Anxiety is 'the dizziness of freedom' and despair is a failure to become oneself; 'subjectivity is truth' means that existential truth lies in passionate commitment, not mere correct opinion.
Critics charge him with irrationalism, fanaticism and excessive individualism, but he became the fountainhead of existentialism.

quiz.question: What was Kierkegaard's main complaint against Hegel's 'System'?
options: It relied too heavily on experiments and observation
It explained world history but left out the existing individual who must decide how to live
It was too pessimistic about human progress
It rejected Christianity entirely
quiz.explanation: Kierkegaard mocked the system-builder who forgets he himself exists; the System could place you in history but not tell you how to live. Hegel was optimistic, non-experimental, and presented himself as compatible with Christianity.

quiz.question: A friend says: 'I never commit to anything. The moment a job, hobby or relationship gets boring, I move on to the next interesting thing.' Which of Kierkegaard's stages best fits this attitude?
options: The religious stage
The ethical stage
The aesthetic stage
The knight of faith
quiz.explanation: The aesthetic stage is organized around interest, pleasure and avoiding boredom, without lasting commitment, exactly as 'A' recommends in 'The Rotation of Crops.'

quiz.question: Kierkegaard published most of his major philosophical works under his own name so that readers would know exactly what he believed.
quiz.explanation: Most appeared under pseudonyms such as Johannes de silentio and Johannes Climacus, part of his strategy of indirect communication.

quiz.question: In Fear and Trembling, what distinguishes the knight of faith from the knight of infinite resignation?
options: The knight of faith gives up what he loves and also believes, by virtue of the absurd, that he will receive it back
The knight of faith refuses to give up anything at all
The knight of faith follows universal ethical rules more strictly
The knight of faith proves God's existence before acting
quiz.explanation: Resignation surrenders and accepts the loss; faith surrenders and at the same time believes it will be restored, which Johannes finds both admirable and beyond his own powers.

quiz.question: What does the phrase 'teleological suspension of the ethical' refer to?
options: Kant's claim that duty must never be suspended
The suspension of a moral rule because the consequences would be bad
Hegel's idea that ethics evolves through history
The possibility that universal ethics is set aside for a higher end, an individual's absolute relation to God
quiz.explanation: Telos means end or goal: Johannes asks whether Abraham's duty to God could override the universal ethical prohibition on killing his son.

quiz.question: According to Kierkegaard, how does anxiety differ from fear?
options: Anxiety is always caused by a physical illness
Fear has a specific object, while anxiety is directed at possibility and freedom itself
Fear is felt only by humans, anxiety only by animals
There is no real difference; they are synonyms
quiz.explanation: Fear targets a definite threat; anxiety is 'the dizziness of freedom,' a response to the open possibilities of a free being.

quiz.question: Kierkegaard claimed that the most common form of despair is despair that does not know it is despair.
quiz.explanation: In The Sickness unto Death he argues that many people who seem content have never become selves and do not realize their condition.

quiz.question: What does Johannes Climacus mean by 'subjectivity is truth'?
options: Every opinion is equally correct
Scientific facts depend on how we feel about them
In matters of how one exists, the passionate, inward way a belief is held is decisive
Only the subjective experiences of philosophers count as truth
quiz.explanation: Climacus is not a relativist about mathematics or history; he claims that existential truth concerns the 'how' of commitment, as in his example of the passionate idolater.

quiz.question: The exact phrase 'leap of faith' appears frequently in Kierkegaard's writings.
quiz.explanation: Kierkegaard speaks of the 'leap' and of faith as a decision beyond proof, but the phrase 'leap of faith' itself is a later summary of his view.

quiz.question: Which later thinker called Kierkegaard's leap a form of 'philosophical suicide'?
options: Albert Camus
G.W.F. Hegel
John Stuart Mill
Thomas Aquinas
quiz.explanation: Camus, whom we meet on Day 79, admired Kierkegaard's honesty about the absurd but criticized the leap into faith as an escape from it.

goDeeper.body:
One lively scholarly debate concerns the pseudonyms. Kierkegaard asked readers, in a short statement appended to the *Postscript*, not to attribute the pseudonymous authors' words to him. Some scholars take this seriously and read each pseudonymous book as a portrait of a limited point of view: Johannes de silentio, for example, explicitly says he does not have faith, so *Fear and Trembling* may be a study of faith seen from outside rather than Kierkegaard's own theology. Others think the pseudonyms are a literary game and that the main ideas are recognizably his. How you settle this changes how you read everything, including the famous 'leap.'

A second debate concerns ethics. Emmanuel Levinas and others worried that Fear and Trembling places a private relation to God above our obligations to the vulnerable human in front of us. Defenders reply that Kierkegaard's later *Works of Love* (1847), published under his own name, makes love of the neighbor central, and that Fear and Trembling is meant to disturb complacent believers, not to license violence.

Finally, there is Kierkegaard's surprisingly modern account of the self as a relation that must relate to itself. This idea, that a self is not a thing you have but an activity you perform, runs through Heidegger's Dasein and Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' (Days 76 and 77), and it also connects with contemporary narrative theories of identity, which say we become selves by telling and owning the story of our lives. You might compare it with Locke's memory theory (Day 47) and Hume's bundle theory (Day 50): for Kierkegaard, the question is less 'what makes me the same person over time?' than 'have I chosen to become someone at all?'

readings.title: Fear and Trembling
readings.author: Søren Kierkegaard (trans. Alastair Hannay)
readings.note: Short and gripping; start with the 'Attunement' section's four retellings of the Abraham story, then the 'Preamble from the Heart.'

readings.title: Either/Or: A Fragment of Life
readings.author: Søren Kierkegaard (abridged, trans. Alastair Hannay)
readings.note: Read 'The Rotation of Crops' and one of Judge William's letters side by side.

readings.title: Philosopher of the Heart: The Restless Life of Søren Kierkegaard
readings.author: Clare Carlisle
readings.note: A beautifully written recent biography that ties the ideas to the life, including Regine.

readings.title: The Existentialist's Survival Guide
readings.author: Gordon Marino
readings.note: A Kierkegaard scholar applies his ideas to anxiety, depression and love in accessible prose.

questions: Is there any principled way to distinguish Abraham, as Kierkegaard presents him, from a dangerous fanatic? Does Kierkegaard want us to be able to?
Is the ethical stage, with its emphasis on committing and choosing yourself, genuinely superior to the aesthetic, or just a different taste?
Can Kierkegaard's account of anxiety and despair survive if you remove his Christian answer to them?
